newsitem.title: UK: EU must encourage use of farm futures - UN expert.
newsitem.headline: EU must encourage use of farm futures - UN expert.

text.p: The European Union (EU) should actively stimulate demand for agricultural derivatives to help fill the gap once government support dwindles, a top United Nations official told a conference on Monday.

Current levels of EU subsidy were not sustainable in the face of mounting budget restraints while the EU plans to expand to the east, said Lamon Rutten, the head of commodities division of the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development.
"Politicians will understand that they can't continue protecting farmers in the same old manner," Rutten told a conference on Risk Management in Agriculture.
"But if they can tell them "We will help you to use other mechanisms to reduce the risks', it's a more acceptable message," he said.

Two new wheat futures contracts launched this summer in Amsterdam and Paris have seen scant interest and traders say the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE), which also plans a new contract, will have similar problems unless it simply lists the world benchmark Chicago grain futures.
Rutten said one factor restraining demand for derivatives was the relatively old age of European farmers who are resistant to change.
"Half of EU farmers are close to retirement. It may be only when the next farmers' generation takes over that the attitude of farmers towards their marketing is changed," he said.
European exchanges should consider strategic alliances between them, rather than each going in their own way, to help streamline the market for agricultural derivatives, he said.

But price volatility was at the doorstep of European farmers and the risks were so large that unless they prepared themselves to use risk management tools they would be wiped out by their competitors.

"Within a decade, they (farmers) will have to learn how to stand and walk on their own, competing for the attention of the consumers not just with their equally pampered co-Europeans, but with producers from over the world," Rutten said.

He added that radical elimination of all agricultural supports would be on the agenda in the next round of world trade talks in 1999 and the EU would be forced to bow to pressure, mainly from the United States. "A safety net will remain, but providing prices that are so low that it is unlikely that farmers will be able to rely on them," Rutten said.
Policy adaptation could provide European conditions sufficiently different from those in place in the United States to help a European exchange to build up liquidity, he said.
